title: Who Gets to Build Drones? Jobs, Hobbyists, and the Skills Gap Behind 480,000 Remote Pilots
sub_heading: Drone certificates are common and the hobby built the technology. What the 2026 numbers say about drone jobs, FPV hobbyists, and why design-and-build skills rarely reach new people.
body_html:
In short: The United States has more drones and drone pilots than ever: 837,513 registered drones, about 1.2 million recreational safety-test certificates, and roughly 480,000 certificated remote pilots (FAA, late 2025). What it doesn't have enough of is people who can build, fix, and point a drone at a real problem. That skill came out of the hobby world, and it mostly stays there. This article looks at what the numbers say about drone jobs, hobbyists, and building, and why the next step is getting design-and-build skills to people who would never find the hobby on their own.

Key takeaways

  • Certificates are common; applied skill is not. In the FAA's 2024 operator survey, 36% of Part 107 holders flew only recreationally and 8% did not fly at all.
  • The hobby is deepening, not widening. New recreational registrations fell from about 6,050 a month in 2023 to about 4,780 in 2025, while the average hobbyist now owns more aircraft (3.8 to 4.9).
  • Hobbyists built the technology. Betaflight, the firmware on most FPV drones, is a chain of volunteer projects, and the founders of both DJI and 3D Robotics started as hobbyists.
  • But hobby knowledge rarely travels. Research on household innovation finds only about 6% of the things people invent for themselves ever spread to anyone else.
  • Design and build is the missing rung between "I can fly" and "I can solve a problem with this," and it's the rung most programs skip.

Drones are everywhere. Drone skills are not.

The market has done its job of putting drones into people's hands. As of November 2025 the FAA counted 837,513 registered drones (453,635 commercial and 371,334 recreational), 1,226,168 TRUST certificates issued to recreational flyers, and 481,760 certificated remote pilots. The FAA's own forecast expects about 628,600 remote pilots by 2030.

So the question for someone thinking about a drone career isn't "can I get a certificate?" Hundreds of thousands of people have one. The question is what you can do with the aircraft once you have it.

What the jobs data actually shows

There is no "drone pilot" occupation in federal labor statistics. The Bureau of Labor Statistics has no dedicated category, so be careful with any salary figure that claims to be one. In particular, the commercial airline and charter pilot median ($123,220 in May 2025) is not drone pilot pay.

What the data does show:

  • Where commercial flying happens. In the FAA's survey of 2024 operators, the most common commercial sectors were real estate and construction, media and telecom, agriculture and forestry, arts and entertainment, law enforcement and emergency response, and education.
  • Drones as a growth driver for technical jobs. BLS projects aerospace engineering and operations technicians to grow 12% from 2025 to 2035 and names "continued interest in drones" as a reason. The median wage was $82,890 in May 2025. These are the people who build, test, and maintain aircraft, not only fly them.
  • A skills gap rather than a pilot gap. With roughly 1.16 remote pilots for every active commercial drone, and over a third of certificate holders not flying commercially, the shortage employers describe is specific expertise: inspection, mapping, data processing, maintenance, and integration.
  • Rules still catching up. The FAA's proposed Part 108 rule for routine beyond-visual-line-of-sight (BVLOS) flight was published in August 2025 and sent for White House review in July 2026. As of October 2026 it is not final, and BVLOS work still runs on waivers. When it lands, the jobs that grow will need people who understand systems, not just sticks.

For a deeper look at industries, see our drone careers article.

The hobby is getting deeper, not wider

The FAA's 2026 forecast includes a quiet but important signal. New recreational owner registrations dropped from 6,053 a month in 2023 to 4,782 a month in 2025, and expirations now outpace new sign-ups. The FAA itself says recreational flying "may be on the decline."

At the same time, the hobbyists who stay are going further: registered aircraft per recreational operator rose from 0.97 to 1.26, and surveyed hobbyists reported owning 4.9 aircraft on average, up from 3.8.

That pattern is what you'd expect from a skill that spreads sideways. Inside the hobby, knowledge moves fast. Someone posts a tune, a build log, or a fix, and everyone in the community has it within days. But the community has to find you first. If nobody you know flies FPV, the door stays closed.

Hobbyists built the stack

The drone industry is one of the clearest cases of users inventing the product:

  • Betaflight's family tree is all volunteers. MultiWii (around 2010) ran a flight controller on an Arduino using the gyro from a Nintendo Wii accessory. Baseflight ported it to 32-bit chips, Cleanflight forked from Baseflight in 2014, and Betaflight forked from Cleanflight in 2015. Today about 700 people have contributed code to Betaflight.
  • ArduPilot grew out of the DIY Drones hobby forum (2007–2009) and now has about 1,400 contributors.
  • DJI and 3D Robotics were both founded by hobbyist user-entrepreneurs without professional financing, according to a 2022 study in Organization Science.
  • PX4 is the contrast: it started as a university student project at ETH Zurich. The academic route and the hobby route ended up in the same place.

That is a remarkable record. It's also a warning. Economists who study household innovation estimate that about 5% of US adults invent or modify something for their own use, but only around 6% of those innovations ever spread to anyone else. Most good ideas stay in the garage.

Why building is the missing rung

Most drone education stops at one of two places: fly it (stick time, often on a ready-made aircraft) or pass the test (Part 107 knowledge). Both matter. Neither teaches someone to design a part, read a wiring diagram, configure a flight controller, or diagnose why an aircraft drifts. Those are exactly the skills that hobbyists pick up from each other and that employers describe as hard to find.

Building also teaches skills that travel well beyond drones:

  • CAD. O*NET lists AutoCAD as an in-demand "hot technology" across 171 occupations. Meanwhile BLS projects only 1% growth for drafters, because engineers and technicians now do their own CAD. CAD is becoming a general skill rather than a job title.
  • Making something that has to work. A meta-analysis of 30 studies (12,585 students) found project-based learning outperformed traditional instruction with a large effect size (d = 0.71). A randomized trial of project-based AP courses raised the share of students earning a qualifying score by 8 points in year one and 10 in year two.
  • Systems thinking. A drone is a power system, a radio link, a control loop, a structure, and a set of regulations at once. Getting one to fly well is an integration problem, which is what most technical jobs actually are.

What a classroom build looks like (how we're designing it)

We're designing a Drone Building course for schools and makers, opening in early access in January 2027. It's a draft, not a live product, but the design choices show what "build" means in practice:

  • Students design and 3D-print the frame for a small 3.5-inch guarded quad: PLA for prototypes, PETG for the final print. A crash costs a reprint, not an aircraft.
  • Two versions of the electronics: one where students do the soldering, and a pre-soldered option for classrooms without a soldering lab.
  • Betaflight configuration on a real flight controller, the same open-source firmware the hobby built.
  • Hard safety gates: props stay off until the failsafe has been demonstrated, and every flight day runs under a Part 107 remote pilot in command.
  • The law as a unit: registration and Remote ID for a home-built aircraft are taught, not footnoted.

A 2026 caution for builders: on December 22, 2025, the FCC added foreign-produced drones and critical drone components to its Covered List, which blocks new equipment authorizations. Parts and drones that were already authorized can still be sold and flown. If you're planning a build or a classroom kit, check that each part's model was authorized before that date.

Help us test it

We're looking for teachers, makerspace leads, and experienced builders to try the course before it opens in January 2027 and tell us where it breaks. Join the Drone Building early-access list and tell us whether you'd build in a classroom, a club, or at home.

If you want to start with the regulations now, the FAA Part 107 course is live, and Unit 1 is free to preview.

Questions answered

Do I need a Part 107 certificate to fly a drone I built?

Not for purely recreational flying. Recreational flyers need to pass the free TRUST test, register any drone over 250 grams (0.55 lb), and meet Remote ID, either with a broadcast module or by flying at an FAA-Recognized Identification Area. Any flight in furtherance of a business, including paid work, needs Part 107. Check current FAA guidance before you fly.

Is "drone pilot" a real job title?

Yes in job postings, but not in federal labor statistics, which is why salary claims vary so much. Most drone work sits inside another job: inspector, surveyor, technician, photographer, first responder, or farmer.

How much does it cost to build an FPV drone?

Parts for a basic 5-inch FPV quad have been priced around $100 (2025), but a complete setup with radio, goggles, batteries, and charger costs several hundred dollars or more. Prices in the US are less predictable in 2026 because of tariffs and the FCC's restrictions on new foreign components.

Do I need an engineering degree to learn drone CAD?

No. Designing a frame starts with measuring the parts you have and drawing plates and arms around them. High school students do it routinely with free or education-licensed CAD tools.
